n: Museum of Astronomy and Related Sciences (MAST)
w: Built 1913-1921 as the National Observatory's new home after old Castelo Hill was demolished, the building now holds interactive experiments, a scaled Solar System, and a chunk of asteroid in its courtyard. Every Saturday night the domes reopen and century-old telescopes are turned over to the public for free stargazing.
s: Century-old telescopes reopened to the public weekly
why: One of the few observatories anywhere that lets the public look through instruments over a century old, free, every week.

w: A ninth-century defense tower once used for imprisonment and torture was converted in 1767 into an astronomical observatory, its cells replaced by instrument rooms and a rotating dome. Historic telescopes, quadrants, and meridian instruments remain in the tower where Padua's astronomers charted the sky for over two centuries.
s: A medieval torture tower turned working observatory
why: Rare case of a medieval prison tower converted wholesale into a functioning astronomical observatory, still holding its original instruments.

w: Bronze instruments the size of small buildings crown a 15-metre Ming city-wall tower: an ecliptic armilla, an altazimuth, a celestial globe and more, some designed with Jesuit astronomer Ferdinand Verbiest. Built in 1442 and used into the 20th century, it tracked stars for the Chinese calendar entirely without a single telescope.
s: Bronze star-tracking instruments atop a Ming city wall
why: One of the oldest observatories on Earth still displaying its original pre-telescopic bronze instruments in situ.

w: A 16th-century defensive bastion of Utrecht's city wall was topped in 1854 with a domed observatory for meteorologist Buys Ballot, who founded the Royal Dutch Meteorological Institute here before it moved away. Beneath the dome, excavators later found the remains of the city's first chemical laboratory, the third ever built.
s: A city-wall bastion turned dome for weather and stars
why: Combines a medieval fortification, the birthplace of Dutch national meteorology, and a rediscovered 17th-century chemistry lab in one small hill.

w: Architect Christian Grosch fused a professor's residence with an observatory dome in 1833, giving Norway's first astronomers a home and a workplace under one roof. The preserved interior still holds star charts, brass instruments, and the quiet study rooms where 19th-century observers tracked comets and eclipses above the fjord.
s: An 1833 professor's house doubling as a star dome
why: One of the best-preserved 19th-century combined residence-and-observatory buildings in Scandinavia, still with its original instruments.

w: Relocated from the city to the Bickley hills in 1965 to escape streetlight glare, this volunteer-run observatory once kept Western Australia's official time and logged earthquakes on a century-old Milne-Shaw seismograph. Its telescopes discovered 29 minor planets and supplied a tenth of the world's tracking data on Halley's Comet in 1986.
s: Dark-sky domes that once kept the state's official time
why: Contributed more ground-based tracking data on Halley's Comet than any other observatory on Earth during its 1986 return.

w: Two generations of the Vrolik family, both anatomy professors, spent the 1800s amassing 10,000 specimens documenting how bodies form and malform: fetal skeletons, conjoined twins in formaldehyde, and skulls scarred by syphilis and rickets. Willem Vrolik's teratology research here won a Prix Montyon from the French Academy of Sciences.
s: A father-and-son collection of anatomical anomalies
why: One of the world's most complete 19th-century teratology collections, built by the two anatomists who founded the field's methodology.

w: Anatomist Honore Fragonard prepared some 700 flayed human and animal cadavers for France's first veterinary school in the 1760s, injecting veins blue and arteries red before he was dismissed as mad. Only 21 survive, including a rider and horse both stripped to muscle, encircled by tiny flayed fetuses mounted on sheep.
s: Flayed 18th-century cadavers still posed mid-gallop
why: The only surviving body of work by history's most extreme anatomical preparator, made for one of the world's oldest veterinary schools.

w: Physician Satoru Kamegai opened this free, privately funded museum in 1953 to raise awareness of parasitic disease after the war, and it now holds 60,000 specimens. Its centerpiece is an 8.8-metre tapeworm pulled from a human intestine, stretched the length of the gallery beside jars of flukes, roundworms, and infected organs.
s: An 8.8-metre tapeworm, pulled from a human gut
why: The world's only museum devoted entirely to parasites, funded purely by donations and its own gift shop since 1953.

w: A 1927 villa confiscated by communist authorities now holds Tesla's ashes in a golden urn alongside 160,000 documents and 1,200 original devices from his career in alternating current and wireless power. Coils, motors, and models fill rooms where guides demonstrate sparking Tesla coils and let visitors handle glowing fluorescent tubes.
s: Tesla's ashes rest inside a golden urn here
why: Holds the largest archive of Nikola Tesla's original papers and devices anywhere, inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

w: The only surviving laboratory Nikola Tesla ever built stands on Long Island, where he planned a 186-foot tower for wireless global power before J.P. Morgan pulled funding and the tower was scrapped in 1917. Rescued from foreclosure and a toxic Superfund past by a crowdfunded campaign, the Stanford White brick lab is now a museum in progress.
s: Tesla's last standing lab, saved by crowdfunding
why: The sole surviving physical laboratory of Nikola Tesla, rescued from a Superfund site by a global grassroots fundraising campaign.

w: A wool comber with no formal training spent seven years, 1774 to 1781, building a working orrery into his own living-room ceiling, driven by a pendulum clock and nine weights above the plaster. The golden planets still orbit at true scale and speed today, calculations so precise they only need adjusting once every four years.
s: A wool comber's solar system, still ticking overhead
why: The oldest working planetarium on Earth, hand-built by a self-taught amateur astronomer in his own living room and still accurate today.

n: Chippewa Falls Museum of Industry and Technology
w: Every supercomputer Seymour Cray ever designed sits under one roof in the small Wisconsin town where he built them, from early Control Data mainframes to the liquid-cooled Cray-1. Cray's own drafting desk survives too, still scattered with the graph paper and number-3 pencils he used to sketch circuits that once led the world in raw speed.
s: Every Cray supercomputer ever built, in one small town
why: Holds a complete lineage of Seymour Cray's supercomputers, built in this Wisconsin town that quietly led the world in computing speed.

w: Maharaja Jai Singh II raised this stone observatory in 1725 on the line he considered India's prime meridian, running through the mythic holy city of Ujjain. Thirteen masonry instruments, giant sundials, hemispherical bowls, and angled walls still cast shadows used to track solstices, star positions, and the correct time for rituals.
s: Giant stone sundials on India's old prime meridian
why: Built on the meridian Indian astronomers once used as their zero-longitude reference, quieter and less visited than its famous Jaipur sibling.

w: A British donor's 30-inch reflector, the first large telescope in Africa or the Middle East, arrived here in 1905 and was soon the only instrument on the planet to record two consecutive returns of Halley's Comet, in 1909 and 1911. The domes and early 20th-century instruments still stand south of Cairo, run today as a research institute.
s: Where the only telescope on Earth caught Halley twice
why: Held the first large telescope in Africa or the Middle East, and was the sole instrument worldwide to observe Halley's Comet in both 1909 and 1911.

w: Founded in 1820 as the Royal Observatory at the Cape, this was the first scientific institution built anywhere in Africa, its 1829 buildings still standing in the suburb that took its name. Historic telescopes fill domes across the grounds, while astronomers here once measured arcs of the meridian and stellar parallax that reshaped astronomy.
s: Africa's first scientific institution, founded in 1820
why: The oldest permanent observatory in the Southern Hemisphere, and the very first scientific institution established anywhere on the African continent.

w: Tucked inside a national park chosen for its near-total absence of cloud cover, this Andean observatory shares its dark valley with a second research station and some of the clearest skies used for astronomy anywhere on the continent. Free tours run by day through the domes, followed by nighttime sessions at the eyepiece under Argentina's driest air.
s: Andean domes under some of the clearest skies on Earth
why: Sited in a national park picked specifically for near-zero cloud cover, making it one of the clearest astronomical sites in South America.

w: Built around 634 under Silla's Queen Seondeok, this squat stone tower is Asia's oldest surviving observatory and possibly the world's, its 362 granite blocks arranged to echo the days of the lunar year. Astronomers once climbed a ladder through its off-centre window to scan the sky for comets and eclipses from the flat platform on top.
s: A 7th-century stone tower built to watch the stars
why: Widely considered the oldest surviving astronomical observatory in Asia, built more than 1,300 years ago under a reigning queen.

w: A wooden dome built in 1926 still houses Japan's largest refracting telescope of its era, a 65-centimetre Carl Zeiss instrument that measured star positions until 1998. Now preserved as a museum on the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan's leafy campus, it walks visitors through more than a century of Japanese astronomical research.
s: Japan's biggest historic refractor, under a wooden dome
why: Preserves the largest refracting telescope built in early 20th-century Japan, still inside its original 1926 wooden dome.

w: Emperor Joseph II commissioned 1,192 wax anatomical models in the 1780s to train military surgeons without cutting into cadavers, carried over the Alps by mule from a Florentine workshop and down the Danube by boat. Sculpted under anatomist Paolo Mascagni's supervision, the collection remains the world's second-largest wax anatomy set.
s: 1,192 wax bodies, mule-carried over the Alps
why: The world's second-largest anatomical wax model collection, commissioned by an emperor and transported over the Alps by pack mule.

w: Lodz's first power station, built in 1907 and expanded in 1929, generated the city's electricity for nearly a century before its turbine halls sat empty. A careful conversion reopened the brick complex in 2018 as an interactive science centre, with exhibits on energy and physics now humming inside the very machinery that once lit the city.
s: A century-old power station, now humming with science
why: Converted Lodz's original 1907 power station into a science museum without erasing the machinery that once electrified the whole city.

w: Peter the Great decreed that any unusual birth, human or animal, be shipped to his new capital for study, building Russia's first public museum around jars of conjoined twins and cycloptic fetuses bought from Dutch anatomist Frederik Ruysch. The 1727 Petrine Baroque building still faces the Winter Palace across the Neva River.
s: A tsar's decree filled these jars with anatomical rarities
why: Russia's first public museum, built from a tsar's imperial decree ordering every anatomical anomaly in the empire sent to his capital.

w: A sandstone tower on the site of an old fort has dropped a time ball at exactly 1pm nearly every day since 1858, the signal Sydney once set its clocks by. Inside, the 1874 refractor is the oldest telescope in Australia still in regular use, housed in domes built when this hill doubled as the harbour's earliest lookout post.
s: A time ball that has dropped at 1pm since 1858
why: Runs one of the few surviving mechanical time balls in the world, still dropping daily as it has done since 1858.

n: Istanbul Museum of the History of Science and Technology in Islam
w: Housed in the Ottoman sultans' former imperial stables beside Gulhane Park, this museum reconstructs more than 800 instruments and machines invented by scholars of the Islamic world between the 9th and 16th centuries. Astrolabes, water clocks, and celestial globes fill rooms devoted to astronomy, medicine, optics, and mechanical engineering.
s: 800 reconstructed instruments from the Islamic golden age
why: One of only two museums worldwide dedicated to reconstructing the scientific instruments of the medieval Islamic world in full scale.

w: Founded in 1545 by the Venetian Republic to grow medicinal plants for training doctors, this walled circular garden is the world's oldest botanical garden still on its original site. A palm planted in 1585, the one that inspired Goethe's theory of plant metamorphosis, still grows inside its own custom-built greenhouse tower.
s: The world's oldest botanical garden, planted in 1545
why: The oldest academic botanical garden still standing on its original site, and the model every botanical garden since has followed.

w: Mongol ruler Hulagu Khan funded this observatory in 1259 at the urging of Persian polymath Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, gathering over a hundred astronomers from across Eurasia under one roof. Their twelve years of observation produced the Zij-i Ilkhani star tables; today a protective dome shelters the excavated tower and instrument platforms.
s: A Mongol khan's observatory that reshaped astronomy
why: Directly inspired the design of Samarkand's Ulugh Beg Observatory and Istanbul's Taqi al-Din Observatory through its influential star catalogue.

w: Buried partly underground in the Swiss watchmaking capital, this museum holds one of the world's largest horology collections, from sundials and water clocks to the precision movements that made this valley synonymous with timekeeping. A working watchmaker's workshop inside still demonstrates the hand skills behind Swiss mechanical time.
s: Buried underground in the Swiss watchmaking capital
why: Holds one of the largest horological collections on Earth, sunk into the ground of the town that became synonymous with Swiss watchmaking.

w: Opened in 1964 as Thailand's first planetarium, this Sukhumvit Road complex has projected the stars over Bangkok for six decades, long before the city's skyline made real ones hard to see. Interactive science galleries surround the dome, covering everything from space exploration to earth science for generations of Thai schoolchildren.
s: Thailand's oldest planetarium, on Sukhumvit Road
why: Southeast Asia's oldest planetarium, still projecting the night sky over one of the region's most light-polluted cities.
